record.tranche_reason: Applies an empirical scaling-law-informed model to ImageNet computer-vision models and reports fitted results; it extends the analysis to vision rather than testing language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study models ImageNet top-1 accuracy as a function of compute, data, and year, and reports a power-law approximation for error. It does not test language-model loss, parameter/token scaling, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The threshold-based compute-halving estimates in Appendix C are the study's own estimates; cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study imposes a sigmoid-product accuracy model on 124 published ImageNet models and uses it to decompose algorithmic versus compute and data progress. The model's form is chosen to approximate a Hoffmann-style power law. It never tests whether a power law describes vision loss or error, for example by comparing against other forms or examining residuals across scales. The Appendix C threshold sensitivity concerns algorithmic-progress halving times, not scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. On ImageNet, algorithmic improvements and compute scaling contributed roughly equally, with data scaling contributing less. Algorithmic progress is mainly compute-augmenting and halves compute requirements about every nine months (95% CI 4–25 months), faster than the 16 months of Hernandez & Brown.
record.recipe_differences: Fits a sigmoid-product model to historical ImageNet accuracy, compute, data, and year data; it does not reproduce language-model held-out-loss scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The estimated compute-halving time changes with the selected top-1 accuracy threshold; the authors say estimates may differ by around an order of magnitude. They also report that limited dataset quality and multiple local likelihood maxima make parameter uncertainty difficult to characterize.

fits_no_version.finding: Estimated halving time of compute needed to reach a fixed ImageNet accuracy varies with threshold: 7.72 months at 0.60 down to 0.67 months at 0.88.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Threshold-based estimates of algorithmic efficiency progress depend strongly on the chosen performance threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Within an assumed scaling-law-style accuracy model, the fitted coefficients are αcompute 0.159 and βdata 0.063. Algorithmic progress doubles effective compute about every 9 months (95% CI 3.55–25.4 months), with no significant data-augmenting effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Algorithmic progress in ImageNet classification is mainly compute-augmenting, at roughly a 9-month doubling of effective compute.

record.problems: The dataset is described as inadequate in size and quality; nonlinear fits can have multiple local maxima, parameter distributions are skewed and non-unimodal, and the authors caution against extrapolating far beyond the observed range. Compute estimates are inferred from papers because most do not report total training compute.

untested.parts: All parts; no language-model loss is measured.
All parts. The authors warn the model may not extrapolate, but they test no extrapolation.
Whether power-law form holds for vision. The form is assumed, not tested against alternatives.
All parts. The authors say a compute term fits better than a model-size term, but give no numbers.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 supports and limits_scope labels and V7 supports label are removed. The study assumes the scaling-law form as a modelling tool rather than testing it. The threshold sensitivity concerns algorithmic-progress metrics, not scaling-law fit choices. The data are cross-paper historical models with estimated compute, not controlled scaling runs.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss and its scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from small-run power-law fits.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation; the study does not optimize or compare those quantities.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count.

The study concerns ImageNet image classification only; it does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer, and its performance measure is top-1 accuracy/error rather than pretraining loss.
Downstream-task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.

It tests sensitivity of a compute-halving estimate to performance threshold, but not disagreements in language-model exponents, compute-optimal splits, parameter-counting choices, or whether language-model curves bend away from a power law.

rows.measure: Fitted log-compute coefficient for effective compute budget, αcompute
rows.locator: Section 5.1, Table 1; Sections 3.1 and Appendix E
rows.note: The fitted model is a sigmoid product, which the authors say approximates a familiar inverse-power form for error; this coefficient is not a directly fitted language-model loss exponent.
rows.check: αcompute is a coefficient of an assumed functional form fitted to cross-paper historical data, not evidence that a power law holds. The reported CI is labelled 95% in Table 1, but the caption says 90% bootstrap intervals, and the interval (0.028, 0.212) is asymmetric. It cannot show V5's effect.
